---
title: Getting Started
description: Install cadjoint and walk the arc from a parametric sketch to a gradient through a solver.
---

cadjoint is code-first CAD in which sketches, constraints, SDF geometry,
meshing and finite-element simulation compose into one function JAX can
differentiate end to end. This page installs it and walks that chain once; each
stage has its own guide.

::: {.callout-warning}
The API is not stable. Expect breaking changes.
:::

## Install

From PyPI, pinned because the API moves:

```bash
pip install "cadjoint==<version>"
```

From a checkout, with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/andrinr/cadjoint
cd cadjoint
uv sync                      # CPU JAX: macOS, Linux, Windows
uv sync --extra cuda         # Linux + NVIDIA GPU instead
```

`uv sync` creates `.venv` and installs cadjoint into it in editable mode. Run
commands through it with `uv run <cmd>`, or activate it with
`source .venv/bin/activate`. Everything beyond the geometry core is an extra,
one `--extra` per name (`uv sync --extra fem --extra tesseract --extra viewer`);
the [extras table](https://github.com/andrinr/cadjoint#install) lists what
each pulls in.

`fem` is the one extra that compiles. petsc4py publishes no wheels, so
`uv sync --extra fem` builds PETSc from source and needs a C compiler, gfortran
and BLAS/LAPACK headers (`apt install build-essential gfortran libopenblas-dev`
on Debian/Ubuntu). Without that toolchain, run the solvers as Tesseracts
instead: their images get PETSc from conda-forge and are published prebuilt to
GHCR for amd64 and arm64, so Docker is the only requirement (see
[prebuilt images](plugins.qmd#prebuilt-images)).

### Supported platforms

| Platform | `uv sync` | `uv sync --extra fem` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux x86_64 | yes | compiles PETSc |
| Linux ARM64 | yes | no: gmsh has no Linux ARM wheel |
| macOS arm64 | yes | compiles PETSc |
| macOS x86_64 (Intel) | no: jaxlib has no Intel-Mac wheel for Python 3.11+ | no |
| Windows x86_64 | yes | no: PETSc does not build natively |

Every "yes" is a fresh `uv sync --locked` and `import cadjoint` in
[`install.yml`](https://github.com/andrinr/cadjoint/blob/main/.github/workflows/install.yml),
run on each push. Where the `fem` column says no, the prebuilt solver
Tesseracts run the same solvers in Docker.

### Playground

The browser app ships in the package and needs the `viewer` extra (`editor`
adds lint and completion):

```bash
uvx --from "cadjoint[viewer,editor]" cadjoint-viewer --open   # nothing installed
uv run --extra viewer --extra editor cadjoint-viewer --open   # from a checkout
```

It opens on a parametric heat sink that declares a mesh, a thermal study and an
optimization. See [the playground](viewer.qmd).

## Parameters

A scene is an SDF tree whose numbers are `Vector` or `Scalar` parameters,
each tagged `free=True` (differentiable) or fixed. `functionalize` turns the
tree into a pure JAX function of those parameters, so `jit`, `grad` and `vmap`
apply directly.

```python
import jax.numpy as jnp
from cadjoint.geometry import Vector
from cadjoint.sdf import Sphere, Translate

p = Vector(jnp.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=True, name="p")
scene = Translate(Sphere(radius=0.3), offset=p)
```

### Compilation cache

`functionalize(scene)(free, fixed)` closes over the parameter values, so
`jax.jit` of it folds every value into the program as a literal: two designs
that differ in one value compile twice. `functionalize_parametric` takes the
parameter dicts as arguments, so the lowered program is identical for every
value and one executable serves them all. With the persistent compilation cache,
a re-dimensioned design compiles nothing, even in a fresh process.

```python
import jax
from cadjoint import extract_parameters
from cadjoint.cache import enable_compilation_cache
from cadjoint.functionalize import functionalize_parametric

enable_compilation_cache()      # ~/.cache/cadjoint/jax, or $CADJOINT_CACHE_DIR
free, fixed, _ = extract_parameters(scene)
evaluate = jax.jit(functionalize_parametric(scene))

evaluate(free, fixed, jnp.zeros(3))                                 # compiles once
evaluate({"p": jnp.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])}, fixed, jnp.zeros(3))    # reuses it
```

The playground's compile worker enables the cache for every request;
`CADJOINT_NO_COMPILATION_CACHE=1` opts out. The stored programs are structured
rather than flattened (a sketch profile is one `(N, 2)` array, a pattern traces
its child once, a shared subtree is emitted once), which keeps them small enough
to compile in under a second; see [program size](meshing.qmd#program-size) and
the [performance notes](https://github.com/andrinr/cadjoint/blob/main/research/performance.md).

## Constraints

Constraints are relationships between parameters, declared on the parameters
and solved separately.

```python
from cadjoint import extract_parameters, functionalize
from cadjoint.constraints import DistanceConstraint, satisfy_constraints

anchor = Vector(jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), free=False, name="anchor")
DistanceConstraint(p, anchor, 2.0)   # p must lie on a sphere of radius 2

satisfy_constraints(scene, steps=8)
free, fixed, metadata = extract_parameters(scene)
sdf = functionalize(scene)(free, fixed)

print(float(jnp.linalg.norm(free["p"])))  # 2.0
```

`satisfy_constraints` projects the tree onto its constraints in place and
accepts under-determined systems, the usual case for a sketch that keeps design
freedom. `solve_constraints` requires an exactly determined system and refuses
anything else.

`extract_parameters` returns the free parameters, the fixed ones, and metadata
carrying the constraint system. The optimizer uses that metadata to project each
step back onto the constraint manifold, so a constrained sketch stays
constrained through a descent. The
[constraints notebook](../examples/constraints.ipynb) works through a
fully determined system.

## Faces {#faces-are-references-not-geometry}

cadjoint stores no boundary representation. The dual-contoured mesh is
extracted from the field at one resolution, so a work plane based on it would
depend on the extraction grid.

The construction tree carries the faces instead. `extrude` spans `±depth/2`
around its sketch plane, so it knows where its caps are and which plane each
profile edge swept; a box knows its six faces; a revolve knows its axis. These
are `Face` objects, and every generated solid carries them.

```python
from cadjoint.construction import PolygonProfile, SketchPlane, Solid, extrude
from cadjoint.geometry import Scalar

depth = Scalar(0.8, free=True, name="depth")
plate = PolygonProfile([[-1, -1], [1, -1], [1, 1], [-1, 1]], name="plate")
body = extrude(plate, depth=depth)

body.faces.keys()        # ['cap+', 'cap-', 'side0', 'side1', 'side2', 'side3']
body.cap("+").origin     # [0, 0, 0.4]  — depth/2 along the sketch normal
body.side(0).normal      # [0, -1, 0]   — the plane edge 0 swept

Solid.box(size=[1, 1, 1], position=[0, 0, 0], name="block").face("+z")
```

A `Face` holds its plane (origin, normal and an in-plane x axis, so a
sketch's horizontal is defined rather than derived from the normal), the polygon
that bounds it, and a `contains(point)` test for world points.

### Work planes on faces

`depth` above is a free `Scalar`, so `body.cap("+")` is not a stored plane at
z = 0.4 but the expression `origin + (depth/2)·normal`. A sketch on it follows
the depth:

```python
boss = PolygonProfile(
    [[-0.4, -0.4], [0.4, -0.4], [0.4, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.4]],
    plane=SketchPlane.on(body.cap("+")),
    name="boss",
)
```

The chain is therefore differentiable:

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def stack(depth):
    body = extrude(PolygonProfile([[-1, -1], [1, -1], [1, 1], [-1, 1]], name="p"), depth=depth)
    top = PolygonProfile([[-0.4, -0.4], [0.4, -0.4], [0.4, 0.4], [-0.4, 0.4]],
                         plane=SketchPlane.on(body.cap("+")), name="b")
    return extrude(top, depth=0.5)

probe = jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
jax.grad(lambda d: stack(d)(probe))(1.0)   # -0.5, exactly
```

The cap sits at half the depth, so the boss on it moves at half the rate, and
the distance at a probe above the boss falls at exactly that rate.

In a B-rep CAD kernel a face is stored geometry that a rebuild replaces, and a
downstream sketch is re-attached to it by a topological-naming heuristic, which
is why reordering a feature can detach the sketch. Here the face is a function
of the parent's parameters: the reference cannot go stale, and it carries a
derivative, so an optimizer moving `depth` moves everything referenced off it in
the same step.

### Tangent planes

Blends, fillets and revolved walls have no analytic face. A point projected
onto the zero set gives a surface point, and the field gradient there is the
normal:

```python
from cadjoint.sdf import Sphere

dome = Sphere(radius=1.0)
pad = SketchPlane.tangent(dome, near=[0.0, 0.0, 0.9])   # plane at the north pole
```

The projection is a Newton iteration in JAX
(`cadjoint.fem.motion.project_points`, the one-surface case of
`cadjoint.zeroset.project.project`), so a tangent plane is differentiable with
respect to the scene's parameters; the pad moves out as the sphere grows.

### SketchPlane constructors

| Constructor | The plane it gives you |
|---|---|
| `SketchPlane(origin, normal, x_axis=None)` | Stated in world coordinates. `x_axis` pins the sketch's horizontal; omit it for the derivation from the normal alone. |
| `SketchPlane.on(face, x_axis=None, flip=False)` | The face's own plane, inheriting the face's x axis — the profile's `u` for a cap, the swept edge direction for a side wall. |
| `SketchPlane.offset(face_or_plane, distance)` | Pushed along the normal. `distance` may be a `Scalar`, so the clearance is a design variable. |
| `SketchPlane.tangent(solid, near, x_axis=None)` | Tangent to the field at the surface point nearest `near`. Horizontal defaults to the world axis most nearly in-plane. |
| `SketchPlane.midplane(face_a, face_b)` | Halfway between two faces. |

Orientation is fixed when a solid is generated; `origin` is the
differentiable part. A drafted or twisted extrusion declares no analytic faces
(draft tapers the walls off their swept planes, twist curves them), so only
`tangent` applies to it.

## Meshing

`cadjoint.meshing` dual-contours the field into a surface. It is written in
JAX, so the continuous half of the extraction (crossing positions, Hermite
normals, QEF vertices) carries exact derivatives, while the discrete half (which
cells are active, how they connect) is frozen per extraction.

```python
from cadjoint.meshing import GridSpec, extract_mesh, save_stl

grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-1.3, -1.3, -1.3), (2.6, 2.6, 2.6), 26)
mesh = extract_mesh(lambda q: jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(q * q)) - 1.0, grid)
save_stl(mesh, "sphere.stl")
```

The output is a faceted solid in every format: one triangle per cell
crossing, coplanar ones merged, a 28-gon standing in for a bore. Details and
the exporters are in [differentiable meshing](meshing.qmd).

### Optional plugin kinds {#pluggable-kinds}

Everything on this page runs from this repository alone: the language, dual
contouring, the lattice feature classifier, faceted STEP/OBJ/STL, TetGen and
Gmsh tet meshes, every solver, the optimizer and the playground.

Five [plugin kinds](plugins.qmd#the-five-in-process-kinds) (`node_map`,
`feature_edges`, `brep`, `step_export`, `drag`) are declared here and filled by
nothing in this repository. They are the extension points for a component that
re-solves a surface against the scene's patch fields with a derivative, which a
STEP whose bore is one cylinder, a traced rather than sampled edge curve, or a
Gmsh mesh whose nodes follow the design would need. Such a component ships
separately; the slots are ordinary `cadjoint.plugins` entry points, so anything
registering them fills them.

With the kinds unfilled, feature edges come from the lattice classifier, STEP
export is faceted, and one thing is refused: a Gmsh-meshed study cannot be
optimized. Its mesh is frozen geometry, and `Optimization` refuses it at
declaration rather than returning a wrong gradient. `mesher="tetgen"`, the
default, is differentiable either way.

```python
from cadjoint import tier

tier.status().flags()    # {'node_map': False, 'feature_edges': False, ...}
tier.report()            # versions and status, for a bug report
```

See [plugins](plugins.qmd#one-contract-two-transports) for the contracts and
[meshing](meshing.qmd#the-gmsh-route) for what a frozen mesh can still do.

## Simulation

Discretizations and physics are declared objects, so the ones a script
solves are the ones the viewer edits and the optimizer re-freezes.

```python
from cadjoint.fem import Dirichlet, HeatFlux, Nodes, SimMesh, ThermalStudy
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Box

bar = Box(Vector([1.0, 0.15, 0.15], free=True, name="size"))

study = ThermalStudy(
    name="bar-conduction",
    conductivity=2.0,
    bcs=[Dirichlet(Nodes.side("+x"), 0.0), HeatFlux(Nodes.side("-x"), 4.0)],
    mesh=SimMesh(name="bar-mesh", resolution=(22, 5, 5),
                 bounds=(-1.1, -0.25, -0.25), size=(2.2, 0.5, 0.5)),
)

result = study.solve(bar)   # needs: uv sync --extra fem
print(result.describe()["range"])   # [0.0, 4.0]
```

Boundary conditions attach to node selections rather than index lists, so
they survive re-meshing and a change of shape. See [simulation](simulation.qmd).

## Optimization

An `Optimization` declares a descent. Its study form makes the simulation
above the objective, and one `jax.grad` call runs back through the solve, the
mesh and the SDF to the `size` parameter.

```python
from cadjoint.optimize import Optimization

run = Optimization(name="cool-bar", study=study, metric="max",
                   steps=3, learning_rate=0.01).run(scene=bar)
print(run.history[0]["objective"], "->", run.objective)  # 4.0 -> 2.939
```

Three Adam steps thicken the bar and lower its peak temperature by a quarter.
Constraint projection is automatic, topology stays frozen between re-meshes,
and `gradient_path` chooses which stages run as [plugins](plugins.qmd): a
mesher, a tet filler or a solver behind a Tesseract, in this process or on a
cluster. See [optimization](optimization.qmd).

## Rendering

cadjoint also renders SDFs directly: a forward sphere-tracing raymarcher for
still images, and WGSL shader compilation for the browser.

```python
from cadjoint.render import Camera, RenderSettings, Scene, render_scene
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Sphere

image = render_scene(
    Scene(Sphere(1.0), camera=Camera(position=(0, 1.5, 5), target=(0, 0, 0))),
    RenderSettings.balanced((240, 320)),
)
```

Rendered pixels are not an inverse-rendering API. See the
[forward renderer](rendering.qmd).
